newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan opens inquiry into Formosa's China project.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan opens inquiry into Formosa's China project.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday launched an inquiry into Formosa Plastic Corp's unauthorised US$3 billion power project in China, with officials vowing to take tough measures against any violation.

The inquiry came after Formosa Plastics chairman Wang Yung-ching on Saturday confirmed that the group had started building a US$3 billion thermal power plant in China's coastal Fujian province in defiance of Taipei.
Economics Minister Wang Chih-kang said on state radio that his ministry had begun investigating how the giant petrochemical conglomerate channelled the funds onto the mainland.
"The Economics Ministry will not neglect its duty. It will swiftly check the funding sources of the Formosa's power plant and handle the case according to the law," the minister said.
Central Bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told legislators that an initial inquiry by the central bank showed the group did illegally send money to China from Taiwan, state media said.
A parliamentary sub-committee grouping legislators from the ruling and opposition parties adopted a non-binding resolution asking the Finance Ministry to freeze Formosa Group's funds.
The ruling has no weight without full parliamentary backing.
"This is a public challenge to the authorities," said Lin Wen-lang, a sponsoring legislator from the opposition Democratic Progressive Party.
The Finance Ministry said it was reluctant to follow the ruling, saying further checks were necessary.

"We cannot freeze its (Formosa's) funds if it complies with government regulations," Finance Minister Paul Chiu told reporters. "If it violates the regulations, the case would be handled according to the law."

The government in March ordered local companies to halt all unauthorised investments in China and vowed to ferret out and punish illegal projects in the face of evidence that Beijing was helping them to keep a low profile.
Authorities can impose fines, repeatedly if necessary, of T$3-$15 million (US$110,000-US$550,000).
Officials and analysts have said Formosa group could easily dodge Taiwan's regulations by channelling the funds through its overseas affiliates or holding companies.

The huge plan has been no secret. In June 1996, the group's affiliates Formosa Plastics, Nan Ya Plastics and Formosa Chemical and Fiber announced plans to build the $3 billion, 3,600-megawatt plant in Fujian province in partnership with Fujian authorities.
The group applied for state approval but publicly backed out two months later after Taiwan president Lee Teng-hui appealed to local enterprises to slow their investments on the mainland.
Taiwanese investment must be routed indirectly through Hong Kong or other third parties and must have Taipei's approval.

China has regarded Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split them in 1949. Nevertheless, nearly 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured some US$30 billion into China since a political thaw in the late 1980s.
